content: The cost of tuberculosis (TB) treatment in Yemen is being analyzed to guide resource allocation across various TB interventions. The methods used to estimate the cost of health interventions, known as costing, depend on the specific purpose of the study. Ideally, cost estimates derived from primary data should be versatile enough to serve multiple purposes, but in practice, costing studies are often designed with a specific objective in mind, which influences the methodological choices, such as the unit of cost reported. Economic Evaluation and Priority Setting Certain cost estimates are used to evaluate the allocative efficiency of one or more TB interventions. Allocative efficiency refers to maximizing health outcomes across competing healthcare interventions within a limited budget. Decision-makers use tools like cost-effectiveness analysis and benefit-cost analysis to assess the efficiency of investments in TB interventions. Cost-effectiveness analysis, for instance, is a critical component in deciding whether to invest in new technologies or prioritize strategies and interventions. This approach is also integral to the development of World Health Organization (WHO) TB guidelines. For example, cost-effectiveness data can inform the design of government or insurer-provided healthcare benefit packages. In low-income countries transitioning to national insurance schemes, these assessments can help estimate reimbursement levels. Financial Planning and Budget Impact Cost estimates are also used to predict medium-term (3-5 years) and long-term expenditures. Examples include using cost data to inform budget impact analyses, national strategic plans, medium-term expenditure frameworks, financial plans for investment cases, and global price tags. These analyses support national planning and global fundraising efforts to increase investment in specific global health areas. For instance, since 2009, the South African government has used cost data to predict the mediumand long-term costs of its national public sector antiretroviral treatment (ART) program, which was then used to advocate for increased ART funding. Budgeting and Price-Setting Cost data can assist health providers or funders in planning their incomes and expenditures. Costs can predict expenditures for specific budget holders and help set prices for specific services. Budget settings may include annual program budgeting for routine health services or investment cases for specific studies or funding applications. For organizations like insurance companies or private providers, budgets involve planning incomes and setting prices for goods and services for the upcoming year, with costs being a core element of this process. Technical Efficiency Analyses Cost data can also be used to explore differences and drivers of technical efficiency between providers or delivery modes (e.g., integrated services, platforms, decentralization levels) for health interventions or services. Technical efficiency analyses are typically conducted by comparing costs across multiple sites or against benchmarks. Technical efficiency involves determining the best way to allocate a limited budget to produce a set of TB services. Cost data from such studies can help identify the minimum efficient scale of operation or highlight areas of efficient or inefficient practices. For example, organizations like WHO, UNICEF, and Gavi use unit cost data to design efficient supply chain logistics systems for immunization activities. Study Objectives and Team Setup The primary output of a costing study is a dataset of unit costs, constructed according to standardized methodologies. For the Value TB study, the output was a nationally representative set of unit costs for delivering TB interventions and services in five countries. The dataset should ideally be disaggregated to facilitate future analysis and decision-making at the country level and by researchers. The core research team, responsible for overseeing the study, defining its scope, and securing funding, should have diverse skill sets. The principal investigator (PI) should have experience in protocol writing, ethical applications, team management, TB, and costing. Field data collectors should be organized, maintain detailed records, understand clinical TB procedures, and report back to the study coordinator. The study coordinator should oversee data collection, provide guidance and training, and identify errors in real-time. A national advisory committee or task force may also be established to provide input during data analysis and dissemination stages. Protocol Development and Ethical Approval The study protocol outlines objectives, study design, timeline, and budget. It should involve cost data users from the start and ideally be developed through a participatory workshop. Adapting existing protocols, such as those in the Value TB Costing Tool Suite, can accelerate the study design phase. The protocol should specify the study objectives, such as estimating unit costs for TB interventions, and ensure that the dataset is eventually made available in a disaggregated form for future use. Sampling and Site Selection Sampling methods vary depending on the study's purpose. Random sampling requires a sampling frame, while stratified random sampling ensures representation of mutually exclusive subgroups. Non-random methods like convenience or purposive sampling may also be used but can introduce bias. The sample size should be determined with a set precision in mind, and the sampling frame may involve selecting countries, regions, sites, patients, or client groups. The purpose of the cost estimation will dictate the most appropriate sampling method and size. For example, financial planning may require data collection from different site types, while economic evaluation aims to compare interventions with comparators. The XTEND study, for instance, aimed to understand the cost-effectiveness of Xpert® MTB/RIF under national rollout conditions in South Africa, requiring empirical costing in a real-world setting.
